newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Foreign investment seen vital for Pakistan stocks.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investment seen vital for Pakistan stocks.

text.p: Arif Habib, the president of the Karachi Stock Exchange (KSE), said on Sunday that foreign investment was crucial because local investors alone could not sustain recent Pakistan share price rises.
"Without foreign investment, it will be difficult to sustain the market at these levels because local institutions and individuals have a limit," Habib told Reuters in an interview.

The KSE 100-share index surged 4.39 percent on Sunday, bursting through the 1,700-point barrier a day before Nawaz Sharif was due to be sworn in as Pakistans new prime minister after his sweeping February 3 election victory.

The index has gained more than 28 percent since January 1 in what analysts say is a sentiment-based rally driven by expectations that Sharif will restore political stability and tackle Pakistans chronic economic problems.
Sharif, who is considered pro-business, has said his top priority will be to revive Pakistans battered economy.
But he may find it hard to offer incentives to industry without falling foul of the International Monetary Fund.
The IMF insists that Pakistan cut its 1996/97 (July-June) budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product from 6.3 percent last year as a condition for a current standby loan.

Habib said the Karachi market's recent rise, relatively low share prices and higher corporate dividends had made Pakistani stocks more attractive for foreign investors, but they were waiting for the new government to reveal its economic policies.
He said foreign investors were interested in boosting their existing share of about 12.5 percent of market capitalisation and were better informed about the market than in the past.
"They know the groups and companies and their profitibility. They will come here if the government gives political stability and restores their confidence," he declared.
But he said investors remained concerned about Pakistan's huge trade deficit and low foreign exchange reserves.

Pakistans trade gap rose to a provisional $2.126 billion in the first seven months of 1996/97 from $2.097 billion in the year-ago period. Foreign exchange reserves, excluding gold, fell to $598 million on February 6 from $680 million on January 30.
Habib said the new government would need to exert economic discipline and slash wasteful expenditure to meet budget targets without increasing utility charges and taxes.
If the market sustained recent gains, it would be able to respond positively to privatisation and new issues, he argued.
He said the energy sector, the largest in terms of market capitalisation, would remain the prime attraction for local and foreign investors because of its high growth potential.

"The index could hit 1,800 points on a sentiment-based rally in the near term, but beyond that there is little upside seen without favourable government economic policies and incentives to trade and business," Habib added.
